Aim and objectives

Aim. To interpret every major Paper B diagram, from forest and L'Abbé plots to survival curves, ROC curves and cost-effectiveness planes.

At the end of this workbook, you should be able to:

  1. Interpret scatter plots in ecological studies, forest plots and L'Abbé plots, and identify the ecological fallacy.
  2. Interpret Kaplan-Meier curves, median survival, the log-rank test and hazard ratios from Cox regression.
  3. Interpret a ROC curve and its area under the curve.
  4. Calculate an ICER and interpret the cost-effectiveness plane and cost-effectiveness acceptability curve.
  5. Interpret a CONSORT participant flow diagram to identify attrition and the analysed population.
  6. Complete all 30 worked challenges, scoring at least 24 (80%), before you open the working.
  7. Turn all 50 flashcards and mark at least 40 as 'Got it' by the end of today's session.

13.2.2.4Ecological studies, scatter plots and the ecological fallacy

Big idea. An ecological study measures groups, not people, so a relationship between area averages cannot be assumed to hold for the individuals inside those areas.
Picture it as judging every passenger by the speed of the train.

Syllabus: Ecological and correlational studies

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 57 · Case reports and cross-sectional studies →

The story in plain words. A fast train carries people who are sitting still. Judge each passenger by the train's speed and you will be wrong about every one of them. An ecological study makes the same kind of leap: its units are areas, countries or practices, and both exposure and outcome are group averages. Such data are usually drawn as a scatter plot, one point per area, with exposure on the x axis and outcome on the y axis. A line fitted through the points shows the direction of association; a point far from the others is an outlier. The danger is the ecological fallacy: inferring that individuals behave like the groups they belong to. In the figure, the areas with more exposure have higher average scores, yet within every area the more exposed people score lower. ((? The plot shows countries with more income inequality have more mental illness. Can we conclude that poorer people in those countries are more often ill? ?)) No. That is an individual-level claim from group-level data, which is the ecological fallacy.

Area means rise together (burgundy diamonds) while, within each area, individuals with more exposure score lower (thin lines). An ecological study sees only the diamonds. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Emile Durkheim's 1897 study of suicide compared rates across regions and religions, and remains the classic ecological study in the history of psychiatry and sociology. Its strength was showing that rates are social facts; its weakness was that individual explanations could not be read from them. In 1950 the sociologist William Robinson showed that the correlation between being foreign-born and literacy across US states had the opposite sign from the correlation among individuals. His paper gave the fallacy its classic demonstration.

From everyday life to the clinic. Ecological studies are cheap and fast, use routine data, and are the right tool when the exposure genuinely acts at group level, such as a policy, a deprivation index or a service model. They are good at generating hypotheses. A scatter of areas showing that places with more adults living alone have more emergency admissions supports an area-level association. It does not show that living alone causes admission, nor which individuals are admitted.

The ecological fallacy: the speed of the train (the area average) says nothing about the stillness of each passenger. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The examiners want the name of the error: ecological fallacy, not recall bias or attrition. They also want the cautious conclusion: areas with more of X tend to have more of Y; never that X causes Y in people. Recognise the plot type: a scatter plot of two continuous variables, not a bar chart or a population pyramid. An outlier is the point that sits well away from the fitted line, and it can drag the line if the sample of areas is small.

Where the exam tries to catch you: ecological studies, the trap beside the right reading. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Rothman KJ, Greenland S, Lash TL (2008). Modern Epidemiology, 3rd ed. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.
  2. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2022). NICE health technology evaluations: the manual (PMG36). NICE.
  3. EuroQol Group (1990). EuroQol: a new facility for the measurement of health-related quality of life. Health Policy, 16: 199-208.

13.4.3Forest plots and L'Abbe plots

Big idea. A forest plot lays every study's estimate and uncertainty along one axis so the eye can see agreement, weight and the pooled answer at once; a L'Abbe plot shows the same trials as raw event rates.
Picture it as a line of archers aiming at the same target.

Syllabus: Heterogeneity, publication bias, funnel plot, quality assessment, meta-analysis, pooled odds ratio and sensitivity analysis

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 66 · Galbraith and L'Abbé plots →

The story in plain words. Imagine archers lined up at one target. Each arrow lands somewhere, and a steadier archer's arrows land in a tighter cluster. A forest plot gives each study a row: the square is its point estimate, the horizontal line its 95% confidence interval, and the area of the square its weight in the pooled result. The vertical line of no effect sits at 1 for ratios and 0 for differences. A study whose confidence line crosses it is not statistically significant on its own. Ratios are drawn on a log scale so that 0.5 and 2 sit the same distance either side of 1. A line with an arrowhead runs off the edge of the plot, which marks a very imprecise study. The diamond at the bottom is the pooled estimate: its centre is the summary effect and its width the pooled confidence interval. ((? In the figure, which study carries most weight, and why? ?)) Study 3, at 57%, because its confidence interval is narrowest, so its inverse-variance weight is largest.

Anatomy of a forest plot on a log risk-ratio scale: squares, confidence lines, the line of no effect and the pooled diamond. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Forest plots grew up in the 1980s and 1990s alongside Cochrane reviews; Steff Lewis and Mike Clarke's 2001 BMJ paper traced the name and the conventions. The Cochrane logo itself is a forest plot of trials of antenatal corticosteroids. In 1987 Kristan L'Abbe, Allan Detsky and Keith O'Rourke proposed plotting each trial's event rate in the treatment group against its rate in the control group. On a L'Abbe plot every circle is a trial, its size proportional to the number of participants, and the diagonal is the line of equality.

From everyday life to the clinic. If the outcome is good, such as response, trials above the diagonal favour the treatment; if the outcome is bad, such as relapse, benefit lies below it. Points scattered widely around the line warn of heterogeneity before any statistic is computed. The pooled totals under a forest plot also let you work out absolute effects. If 25% relapse with treatment and 37.5% without, the absolute risk reduction is 12.5% and the number needed to treat is 1 / 0.125 = 8.

Each study is an archer: a tight cluster of arrows is a precise study, drawn as a narrow line and a large square. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Watch for the inaccurate statement: each study's confidence interval is a horizontal line, never a vertical one. Least influence on the pooled estimate belongs to the smallest square, which is the study with the lowest weight, not the one furthest from the line. On a L'Abbe plot, above the line means benefit only when the outcome is desirable; check what is being counted before you count circles. And the circle size is the number of participants, not the effect.

Where the exam tries to catch you: forest and L'Abbe plots, the trap beside the right reading. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Mantel N (1966). Evaluation of survival data and two new rank order statistics arising in its consideration. Cancer Chemotherapy Reports, 50: 163-170.
  2. Lewis S, Clarke M (2001). Forest plots: trying to see the wood and the trees. BMJ, 322: 1479-1480.
  3. Hopewell S, Chan AW, Collins GS et al. (2025). CONSORT 2025 statement: updated guideline for reporting randomised trials. BMJ, 389: e081123.
  4. Cox DR (1972). Regression models and life-tables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 34: 187-220.

13.5.7The ROC curve and the area under it

Big idea. Every cut-off on a test trades sensitivity against specificity; the ROC curve plots all those trades at once, and the area under it measures how well the test separates people with and without the disorder.
Picture it as a sieve whose mesh you can slide from coarse to fine.

Syllabus: Receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) and AUC

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 96 · ROC curves, AUC and cut-off →

The story in plain words. A sieve with a sliding mesh catches more when the holes are small, but it also catches more grit. Slide the cut-off on a rating scale lower and you catch more true cases (higher sensitivity) but also more people without the disorder (false positives). Slide it higher and the opposite happens. The ROC curve plots sensitivity on the y axis against 1 minus specificity, the false positive rate, on the x axis, one point for each cut-off. The top left corner is a perfect test. The 45-degree diagonal is a test that discriminates no better than tossing a coin. The area under the curve (AUC) summarises discrimination across every cut-off. An AUC of 0.5 is chance; 1.0 is perfect; values around 0.9 are excellent. ((? Which cut-off on an ROC curve has the lowest specificity? ?)) The point furthest to the right, because the x axis is 1 minus specificity.

Left: scores in people with and without a disorder, with three cut-offs. Right: each cut-off becomes one point on the ROC curve; the dashed diagonal is a test no better than chance. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. ROC analysis began with radar operators in the Second World War, who had to decide whether a blip was an aircraft or noise; the name 'receiver operating characteristic' comes from that receiver. Medicine adopted it in the 1970s and 1980s. James Hanley and Barbara McNeil showed in 1982 that the AUC equals the probability that a randomly chosen person with the disorder scores higher than a randomly chosen person without it. William Youden's 1950 index, sensitivity + specificity minus 1, picks the cut-off where the curve bulges furthest from the diagonal.

From everyday life to the clinic. A memory clinic choosing a cut-off on a cognitive screen may accept more false positives to miss fewer cases of dementia; a test that triggers an invasive procedure may need high specificity instead. The best cut-off depends on the cost of each kind of error, not only on the shoulder of the curve. Two screening questionnaires can be compared by their curves: the one whose curve sits closer to the top left, with the larger AUC, discriminates better overall.

A fine mesh (low cut-off) catches every case but also more grit (false positives); a coarse mesh misses cases. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The x axis is the commonest trap. It is 1 minus specificity, so far right means lowest specificity, not highest. The point of best balance is the shoulder nearest the top left, often found with the Youden index. The AUC is not the proportion of people classified correctly at any one cut-off, and an AUC of 0.5 does not mean the test is half as good as the gold standard; it means it cannot discriminate at all.

Where the exam tries to catch you: ROC curves, the trap beside the right reading. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Higgins JPT, Thomas J, Chandler J et al. (eds) (2023). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.4. Cochrane.
  2. Altman DG, Bland JM (1998). Time to event (survival) data. BMJ, 317: 468-469.

13.6.4Cost-utility analysis, QALYs and the kinds of cost

Big idea. A cost-utility analysis counts benefit in quality-adjusted life years, which combine how long people live with how well, so that very different treatments can be compared on one scale.
Picture it as the area of a field: length of road times how good the road was.

Syllabus: Cost utility analysis

Read more in your textbookEconomic Evaluation, QI & Governance, page 28 · Costs, perspective and discounting →

The story in plain words. Imagine paying for a road by its area rather than its length: a long road in poor repair may be worth less than a shorter, smooth one. A quality-adjusted life year (QALY) works the same way. Each year lived is weighted by its utility, from 0 (dead) to 1 (full health), with a few states valued below 0 as worse than death, and the QALYs are the area under that path. One year at full health is 1 QALY; two years at 0.5 is also 1 QALY. In the figure, usual care gives 6 x (0.70 + 0.40) / 2 = 3.30 QALYs and the intervention 5.20, a gain of 1.90. Utilities usually come from a questionnaire such as the EQ-5D, scored against values from the general public. An economic evaluation that measures benefit in QALYs is a cost-utility analysis. ((? A trial measured benefit as QALYs from the EQ-5D. Which type of analysis is it? ?)) A cost-utility analysis, the type NICE prefers because QALYs allow comparison across conditions.

QALYs are the area under a quality-of-life path. Here usual care yields 3.30 QALYs and the intervention 5.20, a gain of 1.90. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Michael Drummond and colleagues' textbook set out the family of economic evaluations: cost-minimisation (outcomes equal, compare costs), cost-effectiveness (natural units such as relapses avoided), cost-utility (QALYs) and cost-benefit (everything in money). The EuroQol Group launched the EQ-5D in 1990: five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain or discomfort, anxiety or depression). NICE's reference case uses it, and NICE's methods manual sets out what costs and outcomes count.

From everyday life to the clinic. Costs come in kinds. Direct costs are resources used in care: staff time, drugs, appointments, travel to them. Indirect costs are lost productivity, such as working days lost, often valued at the average wage. Intangible costs are pain, grief and distress that resist a price. In depression the indirect costs of lost work frequently outweigh the direct costs of treatment. NICE's reference case takes the perspective of the NHS and personal social services, so it leaves productivity out; a societal analysis puts it back in.

QALYs are an area: years of life (length of road) multiplied by their quality (how smooth the road is). Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Match the outcome to the analysis: QALYs mean cost-utility, natural units mean cost-effectiveness, money on both sides means cost-benefit, equal outcomes mean cost-minimisation. Productivity loss is indirect, not intangible. Opportunity cost is the benefit forgone by not spending the money elsewhere, and discounting is an adjustment to future costs and benefits, not a category of cost.

Where the exam tries to catch you: naming the analysis, the trap beside the right reading. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Durkheim E (1897). Le Suicide: etude de sociologie. Paris: Felix Alcan.
  2. Fenwick E, Byford S (2005). A guide to cost-effectiveness acceptability curves. British Journal of Psychiatry, 187: 106-108.
  3. Peto R, Peto J (1972). Asymptotically efficient rank invariant test procedures. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society A, 135: 185-207.

13.6.6The ICER, the cost-effectiveness plane and the acceptability curve

Big idea. The ICER is the extra cost for each extra unit of benefit; the cost-effectiveness plane shows where a new treatment sits, and the acceptability curve shows how sure we can be that it is worth it at each price.
Picture it as a price tag on each extra slice of health.

Syllabus: Incremental cost effectiveness ratio

Read more in your textbookEconomic Evaluation, QI & Governance, page 23 · ICER and cost-effectiveness plane →

The story in plain words. Think of a price tag on each extra slice of health. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) is extra cost / extra QALYs: if a new therapy costs £2,000 more per patient and adds 0.10 QALY, the ICER is £20,000 per QALY. The cost-effectiveness plane puts extra effect on the x axis and extra cost on the y axis. North-east (costs more, works better) is where the decision is made by comparing the ICER with a threshold. South-east is dominant: cheaper and better, adopt. North-west is dominated: dearer and worse, reject. NICE's threshold range has been £25,000 to £35,000 per QALY since 2026, raised from £20,000 to £30,000. ((? Point C in the figure has an ICER of £50,000 per QALY. Is it likely to be judged cost-effective? ?)) Not at the usual threshold; it lies above the £35,000 line.

The cost-effectiveness plane. Points in the north-east quadrant are judged against the NICE threshold band of £25,000 to £35,000 per QALY; south-east is dominant, north-west dominated. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. William Black introduced the cost-effectiveness plane in 1990, giving a picture to what had been a table of ratios. Elisabeth Fenwick and Sarah Byford's 2005 guide in the British Journal of Psychiatry brought the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC) to psychiatrists. A CEAC is drawn from many bootstrap replications of the trial's costs and effects. On the x axis is the willingness to pay per QALY; on the y axis the probability that the intervention is cost-effective at that price. It shows uncertainty, not the ICER itself.

From everyday life to the clinic. A collaborative care service for depression might show a CEAC that reaches only 0.4 to 0.7 across the NICE range: as likely as not to be good value, which tells commissioners the case is uncertain and more evidence would help. Sensitivity analysis tests how far conclusions move when assumptions change, such as unit costs, the utility weights or the handling of missing data. A result that survives every plausible variation is robust.

The ICER is a price per extra unit of health: extra cost divided by extra QALYs, then compared with the NICE range. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Recognise the graphs by their axes: incremental effect against incremental cost is the plane; willingness to pay against probability of cost-effectiveness is the CEAC. A CEAC does not estimate the ICER and does not separate direct from indirect costs. Do not forget the ICER's direction. A negative ICER can mean dominant (south-east) or dominated (north-west); always look at which quadrant the point is in before reading the number.

Where the exam tries to catch you: ICER, plane and CEAC, the trap beside the right reading. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Bland JM, Altman DG (1998). Survival probabilities (the Kaplan-Meier method). BMJ, 317: 1572.
  2. Peto R, Peto J (1972). Asymptotically efficient rank invariant test procedures. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society A, 135: 185-207.
  3. Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.
  4. Durkheim E (1897). Le Suicide: etude de sociologie. Paris: Felix Alcan.

13.9.6Time-to-event data, censoring and the Kaplan-Meier estimate

Big idea. Survival analysis studies how long it takes for something to happen, and it keeps the people for whom it has not yet happened by counting them only for as long as they were watched.
Picture it as a lifeguard counting swimmers still in the water.

Syllabus: Survival analysis

Read more in your textbookStatistics, page 96 · Survival analysis: Kaplan-Meier →

The story in plain words. Picture a lifeguard at a lake with a clipboard. Swimmers go in at different times, some climb out tired, some are called home for tea, and the lifeguard's shift ends before everyone is out. The lifeguard does not pretend that the swimmers who were called home stayed in for ever, and does not throw their record away either. Each one counted for exactly as long as they were seen in the water. That is a time-to-event outcome. Every person brings two facts: a time, and whether the event (relapse, readmission, discharge, diagnosis, death) happened by then. People who leave the study, move away or are still event-free when it closes are censored: we know only that their time is at least this long. The Kaplan-Meier method turns those lanes into a curve. At each event time it asks what fraction of the people still at risk got through it, and multiplies these fractions together. In the figure, 7 of 8 get past month 2, then 5 of 6 past month 5 (the person censored at month 3 has quietly left the denominator), and so on: 7/8 x 5/6 x 4/5 x 2/3 = 0.39. ((? Why is the second fraction out of 6 and not 7? ?)) Because one person was censored at month 3 and is no longer at risk at month 5; censored people leave the risk set without counting as events.

Top: eight lanes, each a person, ending in a relapse (cross) or a censoring (circle). Bottom: the Kaplan-Meier curve built from them, multiplying the fraction who survive each event time. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Edward Kaplan and Paul Meier each sent the Journal of the American Statistical Association a paper on incomplete observations; the editor persuaded them to merge the two, and their 1958 article became one of the most cited papers in all of science. Its gift was a way to estimate survival without forcing everybody to be followed to the end. The method rests on one assumption worth saying aloud: censoring is non-informative. The people who leave must have the same prospects as those who stay. If the sickest patients drop out because they are too unwell to attend, the curve will look better than the truth.

From everyday life to the clinic. Length of stay on a ward is the everyday example. On census day some patients have been discharged and some are still in their beds. A t test of mean stay must either drop the current residents or pretend their stay ended today; both bias the answer. Survival analysis keeps them as censored and uses every day they were observed. The same logic covers time to relapse after stopping lithium, time to first readmission after discharge, and time to diagnosis in a birth cohort. The event does not have to be death, and in psychiatry it rarely is.

The lifeguard's clipboard: climbing out is the event; being called home, or still swimming when the shift ends, is censoring. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The exam's first trap is the y axis: it is the proportion still event-free, not the number who have had the event. The second is reaching for a t test or chi-squared test because the outcome looks like a number or a yes or no; once some people have not yet reached the event, survival methods are the answer. The third trap is treating censored people as events, or as if they never existed. Censored people count in the denominator until the moment they leave.

Where the exam tries to catch you: survival data: three exam traps, the trap beside the right reading. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Begg C, Cho M, Eastwood S et al. (1996). Improving the quality of reporting of randomized controlled trials: the CONSORT statement. JAMA, 276: 637-639.
  2. Bland JM, Altman DG (2004). The logrank test. BMJ, 328: 1073.
  3. L'Abbe KA, Detsky AS, O'Rourke K (1987). Meta-analysis in clinical research. Annals of Internal Medicine, 107: 224-233.
  4. Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

13.9.6.1Comparing curves: the log-rank test and Cox regression

Big idea. The log-rank test asks whether two survival curves differ; Cox regression asks by how much, after accounting for other variables, and it assumes the hazard ratio stays the same throughout.
Picture it as two runners whose pace ratio never changes.

Syllabus: Cox proportional hazards regression, with the log rank test

Read more in your textbookStatistics, page 96 · Survival analysis: Kaplan-Meier →

The story in plain words. Think of two runners on a long hill. Both slow as the hill steepens, but one always runs at half the other's pace of stumbling. You could describe the whole race with one number, a ratio of 0.5, even though neither runner keeps a steady speed. That ratio is the idea behind proportional hazards. The hazard is the instantaneous rate of the event among those still at risk: the chance of relapsing this week, given you have not relapsed yet. The hazard ratio compares that rate between groups. A hazard ratio of 0.5 means that, at any moment, the treated group has the event at half the rate of the control group. The log-rank test compares two or more curves by adding up, at every event time, the events each group had against the number it would have been expected to have if the curves were the same. It gives a P value but no adjustment and no effect size. Cox regression does what multiple regression does for continuous outcomes: it estimates a hazard ratio for each variable while holding the others constant. ((? A team wants the effect of cannabis on time to relapse, adjusted for age and adherence. Which method? ?)) Cox proportional hazards regression, because only it adjusts for other variables.

Left: the hazard rises over time in both groups but treatment always halves it, so one hazard ratio of 0.5 describes the whole follow-up. Right: survival curves that cross, where no single hazard ratio fits. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Nathan Mantel described the test in 1966 and Richard and Julian Peto named it the log-rank test in 1972. In the same year David Cox published his regression model, whose cleverness is that it never needs to know the shape of the baseline hazard; it only needs the hazards of the groups to stay in proportion. That makes it semi-parametric. David Schoenfeld gave analysts residuals for checking the proportional hazards assumption in 1982. Log-minus-log plots, in which proportional curves appear parallel, do the same job by eye.

From everyday life to the clinic. A first-episode psychosis service follows young people for five years. Comparing time to relapse between those who stopped and continued cannabis, with nothing else considered, is a log-rank job. Asking whether cannabis still matters once age, adherence and alcohol are taken into account is a Cox job, and its answer is an adjusted hazard ratio for each. The assumption bites when an intervention helps early and harms late, or the reverse, such as a treatment with an early surge of side effects. The curves then cross, and a single hazard ratio averages a benefit and a harm into a number that describes neither.

Proportional hazards on a hill run: both runners stumble more as the hill steepens, but the ratio of their stumble rates stays 0.5. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The classic pairing: log-rank compares, Cox compares and adjusts. Choosing Cox when no adjustment is asked for, or log-rank when it is, are the two commonest errors. The assumption question has a fixed answer: Cox assumes the hazard ratio is constant over time. It does not assume normally distributed survival times, it does not need the median to be reached, and it handles censoring as a matter of course. Crossing curves are a warning that the assumption fails, not a requirement.

Where the exam tries to catch you: log-rank or Cox?, the trap beside the right reading. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Clark TG, Bradburn MJ, Love SB, Altman DG (2003). Survival analysis part I: basic concepts and first analyses. British Journal of Cancer, 89: 232-238.
  2. Drummond MF, Sculpher MJ, Claxton K, Stoddart GL, Torrance GW (2015). Methods for the Economic Evaluation of Health Care Programmes, 4th ed. Oxford University Press.
  3. Morgenstern H (1995). Ecologic studies in epidemiology: concepts, principles, and methods. Annual Review of Public Health, 16: 61-81.
  4. Petrie A, Sabin C (2019). Medical Statistics at a Glance, 4th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.
  5. Schulz KF, Altman DG, Moher D, for the CONSORT Group (2010). CONSORT 2010 Statement: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials. BMJ, 340: c332.

13.9.6.4Reading survival and cumulative incidence curves, and median survival

Big idea. A survival curve and a cumulative incidence curve are the same information turned upside down, and the median can only be read where the curve actually crosses one half.
Picture it as a glass emptying and a jug filling from the same tap.

Syllabus: Interpret survival curves; median survival

Read more in your textbookStatistics, page 98 · Survival analysis: Kaplan-Meier →Evidence-Based Medicine, page 122 · Appraising prognosis studies →

The story in plain words. Pour water from a glass into a jug. The glass empties as the jug fills, and at every moment the two add up to the same total. A survival curve is the glass: the proportion still event-free, starting at 1 and stepping down. A cumulative incidence curve is the jug: the proportion who have had the event, 1 minus S, starting at 0 and stepping up. Authors choose the jug when the event is uncommon, because a curve that falls from 1.00 to 0.95 hugs the top of the graph and hides its detail. Rising curves of diagnosis by age, or of diabetes after starting an antipsychotic, are Kaplan-Meier estimates drawn the other way up. The median survival is the time at which half the group has had the event: read across from 0.5 on a survival curve, or from 50% on a cumulative incidence curve, and drop down to the time axis. ((? A curve ends at 0.58 after three years. What is its median? ?)) It cannot be determined: the curve never reaches one half, so the median is not reached within follow-up.

The same two groups drawn as survival (left) and as cumulative incidence, 1 minus S (right). Group A crosses one half at 18 months; group B never does, so its median is not reached. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Doug Altman and Martin Bland's statistics notes in the BMJ through the 1990s taught a generation of clinicians to read these curves, including the rule that a curve should be shown with the numbers still at risk beneath it. Those numbers shrink as people have events or are censored, and the right-hand end of a curve, resting on a handful of people, is the least trustworthy part. Curves can also be drawn separately for each birth cohort, so that age runs along the x axis and each line is a different year of birth. That single picture shows the effect of both age and calendar time, which one overall incidence rate would blur together.

From everyday life to the clinic. A trial of a crisis plan after discharge reports readmission curves. The usual-care curve ends at 0.59: more than half have not been readmitted by three years, so the honest median is not reached, and quoting the last time point instead would be wrong. A registry study of children shows cumulative incidence of an ADHD diagnosis rising with age, each later birth year sitting higher than the one before. The likely design is a population-based cohort, and the method is Kaplan-Meier, because children who emigrate or reach the end of the data are censored.

A survival curve is the glass, cumulative incidence the jug: at every moment the two add up to one. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Traps here: reading the median off the last observed time when the curve never crosses one half; forgetting that a rising curve is still a Kaplan-Meier estimate; and claiming that curves which never reach the top or bottom mean everyone, or no one, had the event. Also watch the right-hand tail. Wide gaps between curves with very few people at risk prove little, and a plateau may reflect censoring rather than a true cure.

Where the exam tries to catch you: reading the median, the trap beside the right reading. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Bland JM, Altman DG (2004). The logrank test. BMJ, 328: 1073.
  2. Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.
  3. Begg C, Cho M, Eastwood S et al. (1996). Improving the quality of reporting of randomized controlled trials: the CONSORT statement. JAMA, 276: 637-639.
  4. L'Abbe KA, Detsky AS, O'Rourke K (1987). Meta-analysis in clinical research. Annals of Internal Medicine, 107: 224-233.

13.12.1.1CONSORT and the participant flow diagram

Big idea. CONSORT asks trial reports to account for every person randomised, at every stage, so a reader can see who was lost and judge whether the result still stands.
Picture it as a parcel tracking log from depot to doorstep.

Syllabus: Consolidated standards of reporting trials (CONSORT)

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 126 · Reporting guidelines: CONSORT, STARD, PRISMA →

The story in plain words. A parcel tracking log shows where every parcel went: collected, sorted, out for delivery, delivered, or returned with a reason. A participant flow diagram is the tracking log of a randomised trial. It follows everyone from enrolment through allocation and follow-up to analysis, with a number in every box. The diagram shows how many were assessed for eligibility and excluded (with reasons), how many were randomised, how many received each allocated intervention, how many were lost to follow-up or discontinued (with reasons), and how many were analysed. If 240 were randomised and only 205 analysed, the reader must be able to see where the other 35 went. That accounting is what lets a reader judge attrition bias and decide whether an analysis was truly by intention to treat. ((? A flow diagram has blank follow-up boxes. What should they contain? ?)) The numbers lost to follow-up and discontinuing the intervention in each arm, with reasons.

The four stages of the CONSORT flow diagram. The follow-up boxes, outlined in burgundy, are the ones most often left incomplete. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. The CONSORT statement was first published in 1996 by Colin Begg and colleagues, after evidence that trial reports often left out the very details needed to judge them. It was revised in 2001, again in 2010, and most recently as CONSORT 2025. CONSORT is a checklist plus the flow diagram. It does not tell investigators how to run a trial or which statistical test to use; it tells them what to report so that readers, reviewers and meta-analysts can appraise it.

From everyday life to the clinic. When appraising a trial in a journal club, go to the flow diagram first. Unequal or large losses between arms, unexplained exclusions after randomisation, or analysed numbers that do not match the randomised numbers are red flags before you read a single result. Sister guidelines follow the same idea for other designs: PRISMA for systematic reviews, STARD for diagnostic accuracy studies, STROBE for observational studies and SRQR for qualitative research.

A tracking log accounts for every parcel collected, delivered or returned; a CONSORT diagram must account for every person randomised. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The exam asks which item CONSORT recommends: the participant flow diagram is the classic answer. Distractors such as reporting the costs of the trial, preferring parametric tests or publishing open access are not CONSORT requirements. Know which boxes must always be filled: attrition at follow-up, with reasons, in each arm. Ethnic origin of participants or payments to subjects are not the diagram's job.

Where the exam tries to catch you: CONSORT, the trap beside the right reading. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Youden WJ (1950). Index for rating diagnostic tests. Cancer, 3: 32-35.
  2. Kaplan EL, Meier P (1958). Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 53: 457-481.
  3. Black WC (1990). The CE plane: a graphic representation of cost-effectiveness. Medical Decision Making, 10: 212-214.

Try each one first. Then show the working and read the rule.

Challenge 1 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.2.2.4
Proportion of adults living alone against the annual rate of emergency psychiatric admissions in 14 local authority areas (A to N), with a fitted least-squares line. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
What type of graph is shown in the figure?
  1. Bar chart
  2. Histogram
  3. Cost-effectiveness plane
  4. Scatter plot
  5. Population pyramid
Show the working
Answer: D Scatter plot

Scatter plots show the direction, form and strength of a relationship and reveal outliers. The fitted line here is a least-squares regression line.

Two continuous variables, one dot per area, with a fitted line: a scatter plot. The shaded band is the 95% confidence interval for the fitted line.

Rule: Two continuous variables, one dot per unit = scatter plot.
Trap: Calling any graph with a line a regression output only.
A scatter plot of areas with each residual drawn: area K sits far from the line, so it is the outlier. Every point is a whole area, so conclusions are about areas. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Petrie A, Sabin C (2019). Medical Statistics at a Glance, 4th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.

Challenge 2 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.2.2.4
Proportion of adults living alone against the annual rate of emergency psychiatric admissions in 14 local authority areas (A to N), with a fitted least-squares line. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
What is the most appropriate conclusion from the figure?
  1. Living alone causes psychiatric emergencies
  2. People who live alone are more likely to be admitted
  3. Areas with more adults living alone tend to have higher emergency admission rates
  4. Higher admission rates make people live alone
  5. There is no relationship between the two variables
Show the working
Answer: C Areas with more adults living alone tend to have higher emergency admission rates

The positive slope describes areas. To show that individuals living alone are at higher risk, you need individual-level data such as a cohort.

The points rise from left to right: areas with more adults living alone tend to have higher admission rates. That is an area-level association only; it does not show cause or which individuals are admitted.

Rule: Ecological data support statements about groups, not individuals or causes.
Trap: Moving from area data to individual or causal claims.
A scatter plot of areas with each residual drawn: area K sits far from the line, so it is the outlier. Every point is a whole area, so conclusions are about areas. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Morgenstern H (1995). Ecologic studies in epidemiology: concepts, principles, and methods. Annual Review of Public Health, 16: 61-81.

Challenge 3 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.2.2.4
Proportion of adults living alone against the annual rate of emergency psychiatric admissions in 14 local authority areas (A to N), with a fitted least-squares line. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Which area in the figure is an outlier?
  1. Area N
  2. Area A
  3. Area K
  4. Area G
  5. Area L
Show the working
Answer: C Area K

Outliers deserve a look: different data recording, a specific local service, or chance. They can pull a regression line and inflate or shrink a correlation.

An outlier is judged by its distance from the pattern, not by being the biggest value. Area K lies about 27 admissions per 10 000 below the fitted line, far further than any other area.

Rule: Outlier = point far from the pattern of the rest, not just extreme.
Trap: Picking the most extreme point instead of the one off the line.
A scatter plot of areas with each residual drawn: area K sits far from the line, so it is the outlier. Every point is a whole area, so conclusions are about areas. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Petrie A, Sabin C (2019). Medical Statistics at a Glance, 4th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.

Challenge 4 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.4.3
Response rates in eight randomised trials of an add-on group psychological intervention for depression, each trial plotted as experimental against control response rate. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
How many trials in the figure show a clearly higher response rate with the experimental intervention than with control?
  1. 2
  2. 6
  3. 8
  4. 3
  5. 4
Show the working
Answer: E 4

Each trial is plotted at control rate (x) and experimental rate (y). On the diagonal they are equal. Above it, the experimental arm did better for a good outcome such as response; below it, control did better.

Count only the circles clearly above the diagonal: four. Two sit on the line (no difference) and two lie below it (control better for this good outcome).

Rule: L'Abbe plot: above the line of equality = experimental better.
Trap: Forgetting that above means harm when the outcome is a bad event.
Counting by region: four trials lie clearly above the line of equality (better response with the intervention), two sit on it and two fall below. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: L'Abbe KA, Detsky AS, O'Rourke K (1987). Meta-analysis in clinical research. Annals of Internal Medicine, 107: 224-233.

Challenge 5 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.4.3
Response rates in eight randomised trials of an add-on group psychological intervention for depression, each trial plotted as experimental against control response rate. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the figure, what does the size of each circle represent?
  1. The magnitude of the treatment effect
  2. The number of participants in the trial
  3. The width of the confidence interval
  4. The methodological quality score
  5. The variance within each trial
Show the working
Answer: B The number of participants in the trial

Scaling symbols by sample size stops a small, extreme trial grabbing the eye. Colours or shading can add another layer, such as setting or risk of bias.

Circle area is drawn in proportion to the number of participants, so a large trial is a large circle wherever it sits. The effect is the distance from the diagonal, not the size.

Rule: L'Abbe circle size = trial size.
Trap: Reading a big circle as a big effect.
Anatomy of a L'Abbe plot: each trial is placed at its control rate (x) and experimental rate (y); circle area shows trial size; the diagonal means no difference. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: L'Abbe KA, Detsky AS, O'Rourke K (1987). Meta-analysis in clinical research. Annals of Internal Medicine, 107: 224-233.

Challenge 6 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.4.3
Experimental against control response rates for an add-on group psychological intervention for depression. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the figure, what does each circle represent?
  1. One participant
  2. One centre within a multicentre trial
  3. A trial with a statistically significant result
  4. One trial included in the meta-analysis
  5. A trial affected by publication bias
Show the working
Answer: D One trial included in the meta-analysis

Like a forest plot, a L'Abbe plot shows study-level data, but uses raw event rates in both arms. A wide scatter around the line suggests heterogeneity.

Each circle is one trial placed at its control event rate (x) and experimental event rate (y). The plot shows trials, never individual patients or centres.

Rule: One symbol = one study.
Trap: Thinking each dot is a patient.
Anatomy of a L'Abbe plot: each trial is placed at its control rate (x) and experimental rate (y); circle area shows trial size; the diagonal means no difference. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: L'Abbe KA, Detsky AS, O'Rourke K (1987). Meta-analysis in clinical research. Annals of Internal Medicine, 107: 224-233.

Challenge 7 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.4.3
Response rates in eight randomised trials of an add-on group psychological intervention for depression, each trial plotted as experimental against control response rate. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
What is the plot in the figure called?
  1. Funnel plot
  2. L'Abbe plot
  3. Forest plot
  4. Galbraith plot
  5. Bland-Altman plot
Show the working
Answer: B L'Abbe plot

L'Abbe plots use raw rates, so they show differences in baseline risk between trials as well as treatment effect. They are a quick visual check on consistency.

Experimental rate against control rate, one circle per trial, with a diagonal line of equality: those three features identify a L'Abbe plot.

Rule: Event rate vs event rate with a diagonal = L'Abbe.
Trap: Mixing up L'Abbe and Galbraith plots.
Anatomy of a L'Abbe plot: each trial is placed at its control rate (x) and experimental rate (y); circle area shows trial size; the diagonal means no difference. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: L'Abbe KA, Detsky AS, O'Rourke K (1987). Meta-analysis in clinical research. Annals of Internal Medicine, 107: 224-233.

Challenge 8 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.4.3
Meta-analysis of seven randomised trials of family intervention against usual care in schizophrenia; outcome is relapse at 12 months. Illustrative data drawn for CDA. Fixed-effect, inverse-variance weights.
Which statement about forest plots is inaccurate?
  1. The vertical line marks the value of no effect
  2. The size of each square reflects the study's weight
  3. Each study's confidence interval is drawn as a vertical line through its point estimate
  4. The diamond shows the pooled estimate and its confidence interval
  5. A study whose interval crosses the line of no effect is not significant on its own
Show the working
Answer: C Each study's confidence interval is drawn as a vertical line through its point estimate

Reading a forest plot: find the line of no effect, check which side favours treatment, look at square sizes for weight, then the diamond for the overall answer and heterogeneity statistics below.

Every confidence interval on a forest plot is horizontal. The only vertical line is the line of no effect, at 1 for ratios and 0 for differences.

Rule: Forest plot: square = estimate and weight; horizontal line = CI; vertical line = no effect; diamond = pooled.
Trap: Swapping the roles of the horizontal and vertical lines.
Only one line on a forest plot is vertical: the line of no effect. Every confidence interval is drawn horizontally. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Lewis S, Clarke M (2001). Forest plots: trying to see the wood and the trees. BMJ, 322: 1479-1480.

Challenge 9 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.4.3
Meta-analysis of seven randomised trials of family intervention against usual care in schizophrenia; outcome is relapse at 12 months. Illustrative data drawn for CDA. Fixed-effect, inverse-variance weights.
Which trial in the figure shows a statistically significant benefit for family intervention on its own?
  1. Trial D 2013
  2. Trial E 2015
  3. Trial A 2006
  4. Trial G 2020
  5. Trial C 2011
Show the working
Answer: D Trial G 2020

For a risk ratio the null is 1. Trials B and G have intervals entirely below 1. The others are compatible with no effect, although their pooled result is clearly significant.

Look for an interval lying wholly below 1. Trial B (0.39 to 0.84) and trial G (0.39 to 0.85) qualify; of the options offered, only G does. Trial E (0.46 to 1.05) just crosses 1.

Rule: Significant study = CI does not touch the line of no effect.
Trap: Judging significance by the size of the square.
Only intervals lying wholly on one side of 1 are significant on their own: trials B and G. Every other interval touches or crosses the line. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Lewis S, Clarke M (2001). Forest plots: trying to see the wood and the trees. BMJ, 322: 1479-1480.

Challenge 10 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.5.7
A ten-item self-report social anxiety questionnaire against a structured diagnostic interview, with six candidate cut-off scores marked. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
What is the curve in the figure called?
  1. Funnel plot
  2. Kaplan-Meier curve
  3. Scatter plot
  4. Fagan nomogram
  5. Receiver operating characteristic curve
Show the working
Answer: E Receiver operating characteristic curve

Each point on an ROC curve is one cut-off. Lower thresholds sit towards the top right (high sensitivity, low specificity); higher thresholds towards the bottom left.

Sensitivity on the y axis against 1 minus specificity on the x axis, one point per cut-off, with a 45-degree chance line: a receiver operating characteristic curve.

Rule: Sensitivity against 1 minus specificity = ROC curve.
Trap: Calling the x axis specificity rather than 1 minus specificity.
The AUC is the shaded area: the probability that a randomly chosen person with the condition scores higher than one without it. The diagonal (area 0.5) is chance. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.

Challenge 11 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.5.7
Receiver operating characteristic curve for a ten-item self-report social anxiety questionnaire against a structured diagnostic interview, with six candidate cut-off scores marked. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Which numbered cut-off in the figure gives the best balance between sensitivity and specificity?
  1. 4
  2. 1
  3. 2
  4. 6
  5. 5
Show the working
Answer: A 4

Point 4 has sensitivity 0.86 and false positive rate 0.15, the largest Youden index (sensitivity + specificity minus 1 = 0.71). The optimal point may shift if missing a case is costlier than a false alarm.

Work out the Youden index (sensitivity + specificity minus 1) for each point: cut-off 4 gives 0.86 + 0.85 minus 1 = 0.71, the largest. It sits at the shoulder, nearest the top left corner.

Rule: Best trade-off = shoulder of the ROC curve, closest to the top left.
Trap: Picking the point with the highest sensitivity.
From the ROC points: cut-off 4 has the largest Youden index (0.71), the best balance; cut-off 1 has the lowest specificity (0.15). Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Youden WJ (1950). Index for rating diagnostic tests. Cancer, 3: 32-35.

Challenge 12 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.5.7
Receiver operating characteristic curve for a ten-item self-report social anxiety questionnaire against a structured diagnostic interview, with six candidate cut-off scores marked. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In an ROC analysis, what does the area under the curve summarise?
  1. The positive predictive value
  2. Sensitivity at the chosen cut-off
  3. Specificity at the chosen cut-off
  4. The test's overall ability to discriminate between people with and without the condition
  5. The prevalence of the condition in the sample
Show the working
Answer: D The test's overall ability to discriminate between people with and without the condition

AUC summarises accuracy across every possible threshold. Rough guide: 0.5 no better than chance, 0.7 to 0.8 acceptable, 0.8 to 0.9 good, above 0.9 excellent.

The area under the curve summarises discrimination across every threshold at once. It is a property of the test, not of any single cut-off, and it does not depend on prevalence.

Rule: AUC = overall discrimination: 0.5 chance, 1.0 perfect.
Trap: Equating AUC with sensitivity or PPV.
The AUC is the shaded area: the probability that a randomly chosen person with the condition scores higher than one without it. The diagonal (area 0.5) is chance. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.

Challenge 13 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.6.4
Result of an economic evaluation alongside a cluster randomised trial of collaborative care for depression in general practice, from 2000 bootstrap replications of incremental costs and QALYs. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
The trial behind the figure measured benefit in quality-adjusted life years from EQ-5D. What type of economic evaluation is this?
  1. Cost-effectiveness analysis
  2. Cost-benefit analysis
  3. Cost-minimisation analysis
  4. Cost-utility analysis
  5. Cost-consequence analysis
Show the working
Answer: D Cost-utility analysis

Cost-utility analysis is the type NICE prefers because QALYs allow comparison across conditions. EQ-5D is the standard utility measure in England.

Benefit counted in QALYs from the EQ-5D makes this a cost-utility analysis, the type NICE prefers.

Rule: QALY outcome = cost-utility.
Trap: Calling every cost per outcome study cost-effectiveness.
Name the analysis from the unit of benefit: QALYs make it a cost-utility analysis. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Drummond MF, Sculpher MJ, Claxton K, Stoddart GL, Torrance GW (2015). Methods for the Economic Evaluation of Health Care Programmes, 4th ed. Oxford University Press.

Challenge 14 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.6.4
Cost item (per patient, 12 months)Cost (£)
Antidepressant prescriptions120
GP and psychological therapy appointments640
Travel to appointments45
Working days lost, valued at the average daily wage1,850
Total2,655
Costs counted in an economic evaluation of depression care. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
The table lists the costs counted per patient in an economic evaluation of treatment for depression. Which category of cost is the largest item, working days lost?
  1. Direct cost
  2. Indirect cost
  3. Intangible cost
  4. Opportunity cost
  5. Discounted cost
Show the working
Answer: B Indirect cost

Direct costs fall on health and social care budgets. Indirect costs are productivity losses, valued here by the human capital approach. NICE's reference case excludes them, but societal analyses include them.

Working days lost (£1,850) is the largest item and is lost productivity, an indirect cost. The direct costs of care add up to £805.

Rule: Lost productivity = indirect cost.
Trap: Calling productivity loss intangible.
Sorting the table: resources used in care are direct costs (£805); working days lost are an indirect cost (£1,850), the largest item. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Drummond MF, Sculpher MJ, Claxton K, Stoddart GL, Torrance GW (2015). Methods for the Economic Evaluation of Health Care Programmes, 4th ed. Oxford University Press.

Challenge 15 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.6.6
Result of an economic evaluation alongside a cluster randomised trial of collaborative care for depression in general practice, from 2000 bootstrap replications of incremental costs and QALYs. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
What is the graph in the figure called?
  1. Cost-effectiveness plane
  2. Kaplan-Meier curve
  3. ROC curve
  4. Forest plot
  5. Cost-effectiveness acceptability curve
Show the working
Answer: E Cost-effectiveness acceptability curve

A CEAC is built from bootstrap or probabilistic simulations. At each willingness-to-pay value it shows the share of simulations where the intervention has a positive net benefit.

Willingness to pay per QALY on the x axis and probability of being cost-effective on the y axis: a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve.

Rule: Probability cost-effective vs threshold = CEAC.
Trap: Confusing the CEAC with the cost-effectiveness plane.
Same simulations, two pictures: the plane shows each simulated pair of extra cost and extra QALYs; the CEAC turns them into the probability of being cost-effective at each price per QALY. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Fenwick E, Byford S (2005). A guide to cost-effectiveness acceptability curves. British Journal of Psychiatry, 187: 106-108.

Challenge 16 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6
ResidentUnitDays in unitStatus at census
1Crisis house9Discharged
2Crisis house14Still resident
3Crisis house21Discharged
4Acute ward18Discharged
5Acute ward47Still resident
6Acute ward63Discharged
Length of stay at the census date in two units (a sample of six stays). Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A crisis house and an acute ward want to compare how long people stay before discharge. The table shows a sample of stays at the census date; some residents of both units have not yet been discharged. Which analysis makes best use of these data?
  1. Unpaired t test of mean length of stay
  2. Chi-squared test of stays longer than 28 days
  3. Survival (time-to-event) analysis of time to discharge
  4. One-way ANOVA of length of stay
  5. Pearson correlation of unit and length of stay
Show the working
Answer: C Survival (time-to-event) analysis of time to discharge

Length of stay is a time-to-event outcome. Residents 2 and 5 are right-censored: we know only that they stayed at least 14 and 47 days. Kaplan-Meier curves and the log-rank test use that partial information; a t test would have to drop them or treat their stays as complete.

Two residents (2 and 5) have no discharge date yet. A t test would have to drop them or pretend their stay ended on census day, and both choices bias the answer. Survival analysis uses every day they were observed.

Rule: Time until an event, with some people not yet reaching it = survival analysis.
Trap: Reaching for a t test because length of stay is a number.
Each stay is a lane. Residents 2 and 5 have not yet been discharged: survival analysis keeps them as censored at 14 and 47 days instead of discarding them. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1998). Time to event (survival) data. BMJ, 317: 468-469.

Challenge 17 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6
Kaplan-Meier estimates of time to first psychiatric readmission after discharge in a randomised trial of a crisis-plan intervention against usual care (150 per arm), with numbers at risk. Vertical ticks mark participants lost to follow-up; the rest were censored at 36 months. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In a Kaplan-Meier plot like the one shown, what is plotted on the vertical axis?
  1. The estimated proportion who have not yet had the event at each time point
  2. The cumulative number of readmissions
  3. Time remaining until readmission
  4. The hazard of readmission at each month
  5. The proportion of participants censored
Show the working
Answer: A The estimated proportion who have not yet had the event at each time point

Kaplan-Meier curves start at 1.0 and step down each time an event occurs. The height at any time is the estimated probability of remaining event-free beyond it. Some authors plot 1 minus this to show cumulative incidence rising instead.

Read the axes before anything else: y is the proportion still event-free (here, not yet readmitted), x is time. Each drop is an event; each small vertical tick is a censored person.

Rule: Kaplan-Meier y axis = proportion still event-free; x axis = time.
Trap: Thinking the y axis shows people who have had the event.
Anatomy of a Kaplan-Meier curve: the y axis is the estimated proportion still event-free; time runs along the x axis. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Bland JM, Altman DG (1998). Survival probabilities (the Kaplan-Meier method). BMJ, 317: 1572.

Challenge 18 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6.1
Kaplan-Meier estimates of time to first relapse after a first episode of psychosis, by cannabis use. Vertical ticks mark censored participants. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A cohort of people with first-episode psychosis is followed for five years. The figure shows time to relapse for those who stopped and those who continued cannabis use. The researchers want to test whether the curves differ, without adjusting for anything else. Which test is most appropriate?
  1. Cox proportional hazards regression
  2. Log-rank test
  3. Mann-Whitney U test
  4. Chi-squared test
  5. Paired t test
Show the working
Answer: B Log-rank test

The log-rank test compares observed with expected events in each group at every event time, pooled across follow-up. It gives a P value but no adjustment and no effect size by itself.

Two groups, a whole curve each, and no adjustment requested: that is the log-rank test. Cox regression would be needed only if age, adherence or other variables had to be taken into account.

Rule: Compare survival curves between groups, unadjusted = log-rank test.
Trap: Choosing Cox when no adjustment is asked for.
Choosing the survival method: describe with Kaplan-Meier, compare with the log-rank test, compare and adjust with Cox regression. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Bland JM, Altman DG (2004). The logrank test. BMJ, 328: 1073.

Challenge 19 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6.4
Kaplan-Meier estimates of time to first psychiatric readmission after discharge in a randomised trial of a crisis-plan intervention against usual care (150 per arm), with numbers at risk. Vertical ticks mark participants lost to follow-up; the rest were censored at 36 months. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Using the figure, what is the median time to first readmission in the usual care arm?
  1. 27 months
  2. 32 months
  3. 36 months
  4. 18 months
  5. It cannot be determined from these curves
Show the working
Answer: E It cannot be determined from these curves

Read across from 0.5 on the y axis to the curve, then down to the time axis. If fewer than half the group have had the event by the end of follow-up, the median is undefined and should be reported as not reached.

Read across from 0.5 on the y axis. The usual care curve ends at about 0.59 at 36 months, so it never reaches 0.5: fewer than half were readmitted and the median is not reached.

Rule: Median survival = time where the curve crosses 0.5; no crossing = not estimable.
Trap: Reading off the last time point as the median.
Usual care (burgundy) stays above 0.5 to 36 months, so its median time to readmission is not reached and cannot be read off. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Clark TG, Bradburn MJ, Love SB, Altman DG (2003). Survival analysis part I: basic concepts and first analyses. British Journal of Cancer, 89: 232-238.

Challenge 20 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6.4
Cumulative incidence of new-onset type 2 diabetes in adults starting an antipsychotic, randomised to placebo, metformin or a structured lifestyle programme (modified intention-to-treat population), with numbers at risk. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
The figure shows a prevention trial. Which conclusion does the graph support?
  1. The cumulative probability of diabetes rises with time in every arm
  2. By 36 months nearly everyone on placebo had developed diabetes
  3. The metformin arm lost the most participants
  4. The metformin and lifestyle curves lying close together shows contamination between arms
  5. The active treatments only begin to work after 12 months
Show the working
Answer: A The cumulative probability of diabetes rises with time in every arm

Cumulative incidence is 1 minus the Kaplan-Meier survival estimate. It can only stay level or rise. The gap between arms shows the treatment effect; numbers at risk tables, not the curves, show attrition.

Every curve rises steadily from the first months, and placebo stays highest throughout. Attrition and contamination cannot be read from the curves themselves; the number-at-risk table shows who remained.

Rule: Cumulative incidence curves rise; they show risk accumulating, not drop-out.
Trap: Over-reading curve shapes as evidence of drop-out or contamination.
Cumulative incidence (1 minus Kaplan-Meier) can only rise. The gap between arms is the treatment effect; attrition lives in the numbers at risk. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1998). Time to event (survival) data. BMJ, 317: 468-469.

Challenge 21 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6.4
First recorded ADHD diagnoses in three two-year birth cohorts from a national birth register followed to the end of 2014. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
What does the figure show?
  1. Survival time after an ADHD diagnosis
  2. Prevalence of ADHD in three countries
  3. Delay between symptom onset and diagnosis
  4. Cumulative incidence of ADHD diagnosis by age, shown separately for each birth cohort
  5. Annual incidence of ADHD across three calendar decades
Show the working
Answer: D Cumulative incidence of ADHD diagnosis by age, shown separately for each birth cohort

Each curve is a Kaplan-Meier type estimate of the proportion diagnosed by each age. Later cohorts lie higher at every age, suggesting rising diagnosis over time, and stop earlier because they have been followed for fewer years.

The x axis is age, not calendar year, and each line is a separate birth cohort. That combination identifies cumulative incidence by birth cohort.

Rule: Lines by birth year, x axis age, y cumulative = cumulative incidence by birth cohort.
Trap: Reading the x axis as calendar years.
A Lexis diagram: each birth cohort ages along a diagonal and is cut off when the data end, so later cohorts are followed to younger ages. Plotting by age and by cohort separates the two effects. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1998). Time to event (survival) data. BMJ, 317: 468-469.

Challenge 22 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6.4
Cumulative incidence of a first recorded ADHD diagnosis by age, estimated separately for three two-year birth cohorts from a national birth register followed to the end of 2014. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Which design best describes the study behind the figure?
  1. Case-control study
  2. Ecological study
  3. Population-based cohort study
  4. Cross-sectional survey
  5. Case series
Show the working
Answer: C Population-based cohort study

Incidence needs a defined population at risk followed through time. Registers make retrospective (historical) cohorts possible, because the data were recorded prospectively as children grew up.

Whole birth cohorts were identified first and followed forward for a first diagnosis, giving a denominator and new cases: a population-based cohort, assembled from records kept as the children grew.

Rule: Follow people from a start point and count new events = cohort.
Trap: Calling any register study case-control.
The direction of travel identifies the design: start from a whole population and follow it forward for new diagnoses. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Rothman KJ, Greenland S, Lash TL (2008). Modern Epidemiology, 3rd ed. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Challenge 23 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.12.1.1
Participant flow diagram submitted with a trial report of peer support after self-harm presentations. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A trial report includes the participant flow diagram shown. What should always appear in the blank boxes?
  1. Total cost of the trial
  2. Ethnic breakdown of participants
  3. Payments made to participants
  4. Results of the blinding check
  5. Numbers lost to follow-up and discontinuing in each arm, with reasons
Show the working
Answer: E Numbers lost to follow-up and discontinuing in each arm, with reasons

Here 120 were allocated to each arm but only 96 and 109 were analysed. The diagram must account for the missing 24 and 11 so readers can judge attrition bias.

In the figure 120 were allocated to each arm but only 96 and 109 were analysed. The blank boxes must show where the missing 24 and 11 went, with reasons, so attrition bias can be judged.

Rule: CONSORT flow diagram = enrolment, allocation, follow-up (losses with reasons), analysis.
Trap: Accepting a flow diagram that omits losses to follow-up.
The blank boxes completed: each arm shows how many were lost to follow-up or discontinued, with reasons, so 120 minus 24 = 96 and 120 minus 11 = 109 can be checked (illustrative breakdown). Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Schulz KF, Altman DG, Moher D, for the CONSORT Group (2010). CONSORT 2010 Statement: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials. BMJ, 340: c332.

Challenge 24 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.2.2.4
Proportion of adults living alone against the annual rate of emergency psychiatric admissions in 14 local authority areas (A to N), with a fitted least-squares line. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Which error most threatens interpretation of the study in the figure?
  1. Ecological fallacy
  2. Recall bias
  3. Attrition bias
  4. Publication bias
  5. Lead-time bias
Show the working
Answer: A Ecological fallacy

It may be that within each area the people admitted do not live alone; the link could run through deprivation or housing. Robinson showed group correlations can differ greatly from individual ones.

Each point is a whole area, so the main hazard is the ecological fallacy: assuming the area-level link holds for the individuals inside the areas.

Rule: Ecological study = risk of ecological fallacy.
Trap: Calling it confounding only, without naming the ecological fallacy.
The ecological fallacy in one picture: area P has more people living alone and more admissions, yet the individuals admitted are the ones who do not live alone. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Robinson WS (1950). Ecological correlations and the behavior of individuals. American Sociological Review, 15: 351-357.

Challenge 25 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.4.3
Meta-analysis of seven randomised trials of family intervention against usual care in schizophrenia; outcome is relapse at 12 months. Illustrative data drawn for CDA. Fixed-effect, inverse-variance weights.
Which trial in the figure has least influence on the pooled estimate?
  1. Trial F 2018
  2. Trial D 2013
  3. Trial C 2011
  4. Trial A 2006
  5. Trial B 2009
Show the working
Answer: A Trial F 2018

Inverse-variance weights favour large, precise trials. A tiny trial with few events gets a small square and a wide interval and barely moves the diamond.

Weight is the inverse of the variance. Trial F has only 7 events in 29 people, the widest interval and the smallest weight (1.9%), so it shifts the pooled estimate least.

Rule: Least influence = smallest weight = smallest square.
Trap: Choosing the trial with the most extreme estimate.
Weight is 1 / variance: small trials with few events have wide intervals and tiny weights. Trial F (1.9%) moves the pooled estimate least. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Higgins JPT, Thomas J, Chandler J et al. (eds) (2023). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.4. Cochrane.

Challenge 26 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.4.3
Meta-analysis of seven randomised trials of family intervention against usual care in schizophrenia; outcome is relapse at 12 months. Illustrative data drawn for CDA. Fixed-effect, inverse-variance weights.
Two trials in the figure have an arrow at the end of their confidence interval line. What does this indicate?
  1. Their point estimates are larger than the others
  2. They had longer follow-up
  3. They enrolled the most participants
  4. They were excluded from the pooled analysis
  5. Their confidence intervals extend beyond the plotted scale, so their estimates are imprecise
Show the working
Answer: E Their confidence intervals extend beyond the plotted scale, so their estimates are imprecise

Small trials with few events produce wide intervals. Rather than stretching the axis for everyone, the plot truncates the line and adds an arrow.

Trials C and F have lower confidence limits of 0.27 and 0.19, below the left edge of the axis at 0.33. The arrow marks an interval that continues off the plot.

Rule: Arrow on a CI line = interval runs off the scale = imprecise.
Trap: Thinking the arrow shows direction of effect.
On a wider axis the full intervals of trials C and F are visible: they run beyond 0.33, which is why the original plot ends them with arrows. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Lewis S, Clarke M (2001). Forest plots: trying to see the wood and the trees. BMJ, 322: 1479-1480.

Challenge 27 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.4.3
Meta-analysis of seven randomised trials of family intervention against usual care in schizophrenia; outcome is relapse at 12 months. Illustrative data drawn for CDA. Fixed-effect, inverse-variance weights.
Using the pooled totals in the figure, what is the absolute risk reduction in relapse with family intervention?
  1. 33%
  2. 12.5%
  3. 25%
  4. 37.5%
  5. 0.67
Show the working
Answer: B 12.5%

Pooled totals give an approximate absolute effect: 0.375 minus 0.25 = 0.125. Formal meta-analyses usually apply the pooled relative effect to a chosen baseline risk.

Relapse risk with usual care is 213 / 568 = 0.375; with family intervention 140 / 560 = 0.25. The absolute risk reduction is 0.375 minus 0.25 = 0.125, or 12.5%.

Rule: ARR = control event rate minus experimental event rate.
Trap: Giving the relative risk reduction when the absolute is asked.
The pooled totals scaled to 200 people per arm: 75 versus 50 relapses. The 25 avoided (gold) give an absolute risk reduction of 12.5% and NNT = 1 / 0.125 = 8. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

Challenge 28 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.4.3
Meta-analysis of seven randomised trials of family intervention against usual care in schizophrenia; outcome is relapse at 12 months. Illustrative data drawn for CDA. Fixed-effect, inverse-variance weights.
Using the pooled totals in the figure, how many patients need family intervention rather than usual care to prevent one relapse at 12 months?
  1. 3
  2. 8
  3. 4
  4. 12
  5. 67
Show the working
Answer: B 8

With ARR 0.125, about one relapse is prevented for every eight people treated. Always use the absolute, not the relative, reduction.

NNT = 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.125 = 8. About eight people need family intervention rather than usual care to prevent one relapse at 12 months.

Rule: NNT = 1 / ARR (round up).
Trap: Inverting the relative risk reduction.
The pooled totals scaled to 200 people per arm: 75 versus 50 relapses. The 25 avoided (gold) give an absolute risk reduction of 12.5% and NNT = 1 / 0.125 = 8. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

Challenge 29 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.5.7
Receiver operating characteristic curve for a ten-item self-report social anxiety questionnaire against a structured diagnostic interview, with six candidate cut-off scores marked. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Which numbered cut-off in the figure has the lowest specificity?
  1. 6
  2. 4
  3. 1
  4. 3
  5. 2
Show the working
Answer: C 1

Because the x axis is the false positive rate, specificity falls as you move right. The lowest threshold labels the most people positive, giving the highest sensitivity and lowest specificity.

Specificity is 1 minus the x value. Point 1 sits furthest right (false positive rate 0.85), so its specificity is only 0.15, the lowest on the curve.

Rule: x axis = 1 minus specificity: furthest right = lowest specificity.
Trap: Reading the x axis as specificity itself.
From the ROC points: cut-off 4 has the largest Youden index (0.71), the best balance; cut-off 1 has the lowest specificity (0.15). Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Akobeng AK (2007). Understanding diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic curves. Acta Paediatrica, 96: 644-647.

Challenge 30 · 13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.6.6
Result of an economic evaluation alongside a cluster randomised trial of collaborative care for depression in general practice, from 2000 bootstrap replications of incremental costs and QALYs. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
What is the main purpose of the graph in the figure?
  1. To calculate the ICER itself
  2. To show the uncertainty around whether the intervention is cost-effective at different thresholds
  3. To separate direct from indirect costs
  4. To show the effect of drop-out on costs
  5. To give the confidence interval of the QALY gain
Show the working
Answer: B To show the uncertainty around whether the intervention is cost-effective at different thresholds

Reading at the NICE range: the probability is about 0.41 at 25,000 pounds and 0.66 at 35,000 pounds per QALY, so the case for funding is uncertain.

Read the curve at the NICE range: about 0.41 at £25,000 and 0.66 at £35,000 per QALY. The decision is uncertain, which is exactly what a CEAC is designed to show.

Rule: CEAC = how sure we are the intervention is good value at each threshold.
Trap: Thinking the curve gives the ICER value.
Same simulations, two pictures: the plane shows each simulated pair of extra cost and extra QALYs; the CEAC turns them into the probability of being cost-effective at each price per QALY. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Fenwick E, Byford S (2005). A guide to cost-effectiveness acceptability curves. British Journal of Psychiatry, 187: 106-108.
