Tap a card to turn it. Each card is one concept. Answer it out loud, then turn it: the answer, why, what to remember, the trap and why the other options are wrong.

CARD 1
Cumulative incidence of a first recorded ADHD diagnosis by age, estimated separately for three two-year birth cohorts from a national birth register followed to the end of 2014. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6

The curves in the figure handle children who emigrated or whose follow-up ended before diagnosis.

Which method was most likely used to estimate them?
  1. Receiver operating characteristic analysis
  2. Linear regression of diagnosis on age
  3. Kaplan-Meier estimation
  4. Meta-regression
  5. Spearman correlation
C) Kaplan-Meier estimation

Remember. Cumulative incidence with censored follow-up = 1 minus Kaplan-Meier.

Trap. Missing that cumulative incidence curves are inverted survival curves.

Why not the others.
A) Receiver operating characteristic analysis: ROC analysis evaluates test cut-offs, not time to diagnosis.
B) Linear regression of diagnosis on age: Ignores censoring and treats a binary event as continuous.

Cumulative incidence of a first recorded ADHD diagnosis by age, estimated separately for three two-year birth cohorts from a national birth register followed to the end of 2014. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6.4
What is the main advantage of presenting the data as in the figure, rather than as one overall incidence rate?
A) It shows how both age and year of birth affect cumulative incidence

Remember. Curves by birth cohort against age = separates age effects from cohort effects.

Trap. Assuming the graph proves a true rise in disorder rather than in diagnosis.

Why not the others.
B) It shows the age at which half of all children are diagnosed: No curve approaches half the population, so this is not shown.
C) It removes the effect of changing diagnostic practice: It may reveal a cohort effect, but it does not remove one.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 3
13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6
What is the outcome variable that survival analysis is built around?
E) The time from a defined start until the event of interest, with event status

Remember. Survival analysis outcome = time to event plus whether it occurred.

Trap. Assuming survival analysis is only about mortality.

Why not the others.
A) The proportion responding at the end of the trial: That is a binary outcome analysed with risk ratios or chi-squared.
B) The mean symptom score at follow-up: A continuous outcome for t tests or ANCOVA.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 4
13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6.1

In the same cohort, the team now wants to estimate the effect of continued cannabis use on time to relapse after accounting for age, antipsychotic adherence and alcohol use.

Which method should they use?
D) Cox proportional hazards regression

Remember. Time-to-event plus adjustment for confounders = Cox regression.

Trap. Thinking Kaplan-Meier can adjust for confounders.

Why not the others.
A) Log-rank test: Compares groups but cannot adjust for other variables.
B) Kaplan-Meier estimation: Describes survival curves; it does not adjust for covariates.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 5
13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.12.1.1
Which is a recommendation of the CONSORT statement for reporting randomised trials?
  1. Include a diagram showing the flow of participants through each stage
  2. Publish the trial in an open-access journal
  3. Use parametric tests wherever possible
  4. Post anonymised individual participant data publicly
  5. State the full cost of running the trial
A) Include a diagram showing the flow of participants through each stage

Remember. CONSORT = checklist plus participant flow diagram for RCTs.

Trap. Confusing CONSORT with PRISMA or STROBE.

Why not the others.
B) Publish the trial in an open-access journal: Desirable, but not a CONSORT item.
C) Use parametric tests wherever possible: CONSORT does not prescribe particular tests.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 6
13.14 Prognosis, survival and reading research graphs · 13.9.6.1
Before reporting a single hazard ratio from a Cox model, which assumption should the analysts check?
B) The ratio of hazards between groups stays constant over follow-up

Remember. Cox assumption = proportional hazards, a constant hazard ratio over time.

Trap. Believing Cox needs normally distributed survival times.

Why not the others.
A) Survival times are normally distributed: Cox regression is semi-parametric; it makes no assumption about the shape of the baseline hazard.
C) The survival curves cross during follow-up: Crossing curves suggest the assumption is violated, not met.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 7
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.1

A trainee wants a single source that condenses forty scattered trials of exercise for depression into a transparent, reproducible summary.

Which description best fits a systematic review?
B) An observational study of existing studies, using explicit methods to find, appraise and summarise them

Remember. Systematic review = secondary research that treats studies as its unit of observation.

Trap. Calling every review 'systematic'; narrative reviews lack explicit, reproducible methods.

Why not the others.
A) A new randomised trial that recruits participants from previous trials: A systematic review collects no new primary data and randomises no one.
C) An expert's narrative summary of the studies they consider most important: That is a narrative review; selection is not systematic or reproducible.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 8
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.2

A protocol for a systematic review of lithium in older adults lists its planned stages.

Which stage does NOT belong in a systematic review?
D) Randomly allocating participants to lithium or placebo

Remember. Review stages: specify, identify, appraise, synthesise. No randomisation.

Trap. Confusing a review of RCTs with running an RCT.

Why not the others.
A) Stating the question and eligibility criteria in advance: A pre-specified question and eligibility criteria are the first stage.
B) Searching several databases and the grey literature: Identifying the evidence is a core stage.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 9
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.2

A team planning a review of psychosocial interventions for gambling disorder drafts its search strategy.

Which statement about the strategy is INCORRECT?
  1. Restricting the search to peer-reviewed journal articles keeps the evidence unbiased
  2. One electronic database alone is not enough
  3. Studies in languages other than English should be sought
  4. Trial registers and conference abstracts should be searched
  5. The search should be comprehensive and reproducible
A) Restricting the search to peer-reviewed journal articles keeps the evidence unbiased

Remember. Search wide: several databases, all languages, published and unpublished.

Trap. Thinking peer review guarantees an unbiased evidence base.

Why not the others.
B) One electronic database alone is not enough: True: databases index different journals; several are needed.
C) Studies in languages other than English should be sought: True: language restriction can bias the pooled estimate.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 10
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.2
Which of the following is NOT an essential requirement for carrying out a meta-analysis?
  1. An exhaustive literature search
  2. Pre-stated inclusion and exclusion criteria
  3. The lead reviewer being a recognised expert in the clinical field
  4. Systematic extraction of data from each included study
  5. Statistical pooling of the recorded data
C) The lead reviewer being a recognised expert in the clinical field

Remember. Meta-analysis needs method (search, criteria, extraction, statistics), not authority.

Trap. Equating expert opinion with rigour.

Why not the others.
A) An exhaustive literature search: Essential: without a full search the pooled result may be biased.
B) Pre-stated inclusion and exclusion criteria: Essential: eligibility must be set before studies are seen.

TrialnMean episodesSDRange
Trial 1842.13.40 to 19

Trial 3662.74.00 to 22
Number of self-harm episodes over six months, as reported by three trials included in a review. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.3

The table shows the number of self-harm episodes over six months in three trials included in a review.

What does this pattern most likely indicate?
  1. The outcome data are positively skewed
  2. A calculation error has been made in each trial
  3. Meta-analysis is impossible
  4. There is serious publication bias
  5. The trials were too small
A) The outcome data are positively skewed

Remember. Non-negative variable with SD > mean = skewed.

Trap. Assuming a large SD means an error.

Why not the others.
B) A calculation error has been made in each trial: This pattern is expected for skewed counts; it is not an error.
C) Meta-analysis is impossible: Pooling is still possible, for example after log transformation or dichotomising.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 12
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.3

A review of an antidepressant in bipolar depression is criticised for heterogeneity.

Which of the following would NOT help identify statistical heterogeneity?
  1. Cochran's Q test
  2. The I-squared statistic
  3. A Galbraith (radial) plot
  4. A L'Abbé plot of event rates
  5. Having two reviewers independently screen abstracts
E) Having two reviewers independently screen abstracts

Remember. Heterogeneity tools: eyeball forest plot, Q, I-squared, Galbraith, L'Abbé.

Trap. Choosing a quality-control step for a heterogeneity question.

Why not the others.
A) Cochran's Q test: Q tests whether variation exceeds chance.
B) The I-squared statistic: I-squared gives the percentage of variation due to heterogeneity.

CARD 13
Executive function in adults with ADHD versus healthy controls, grouped by type of task. Negative values mean poorer performance in ADHD; teal line = no difference; heterogeneity is shown under each subtotal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.3
From the figure, what can be concluded about the two task-type subgroups?
A) There is no significant difference between the subgroups

Remember. Overlapping subgroup diamonds + non-significant interaction = no demonstrated subgroup difference.

Trap. Claiming homogeneity from a non-significant test.

Why not the others.
B) The subgroups are proven to be identical: Non-significance does not prove equivalence.
C) Paper-based tasks show a significantly larger deficit: The paper-based subtotal is slightly smaller, and the difference is not significant.

13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.4

A meta-analysis of the ten published trials in the table finds that a new antipsychotic reduces relapse significantly more than an established drug. A reviewer asks how many unpublished null studies would have to exist to make the pooled result…

What is this quantity called?
C) Fail-safe N

Remember. File drawer problem = fail-safe N.

Trap. Confusing it with a heterogeneity statistic.

Why not the others.
A) Cochran's Q: Q tests heterogeneity.
B) I-squared: I-squared quantifies heterogeneity.

13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.4
Which plot is designed to detect publication bias in a meta-analysis?
C) Funnel plot

Remember. Publication bias = asymmetrical funnel.

Trap. Assuming asymmetry always means publication bias.

Why not the others.
A) Kaplan-Meier plot: Kaplan-Meier plots show time to event.
B) ROC curve: ROC curves describe diagnostic accuracy.

CARD 16
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.4
When assessing publication bias in a systematic review, which of the following is NOT a method for detecting it?
  1. Inspecting a funnel plot
  2. Calculating a fail-safe N
  3. Comparing published results with registered but unpublished trials
  4. Applying Egger's regression test
  5. Examining the width of the pooled confidence interval
E) Examining the width of the pooled confidence interval

Remember. Pooled CI = precision, not publication bias.

Trap. Equating precision with freedom from bias.

Why not the others.
A) Inspecting a funnel plot: Funnel plot asymmetry is the standard visual check.
B) Calculating a fail-safe N: Fail-safe N estimates how robust the result is to missing studies.

CARD 17
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.5

A meta-analyst chooses a fixed-effect model.

What is the key assumption behind that choice?
C) All studies estimate one common true effect, and differences between them arise from chance

Remember. Fixed effect: one true effect + chance. Random effects: a distribution of true effects.

Trap. Thinking fixed effect means the results are identical.

Why not the others.
A) Each study estimates a different true effect drawn from a distribution: That is the random-effects assumption.
B) Differences between studies reflect the rating scales used: Methodological differences are a reason to doubt a fixed-effect model, not its assumption.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 18
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.3.1.9
Which statement about risk ratios in a meta-analysis is INACCURATE?
  1. The risk ratio is the risk in the treated group divided by the risk in the control group
  2. A risk ratio below 1 indicates no difference between the groups
  3. Risk ratios are usually reported with confidence intervals
  4. Risk ratios are used to summarise treatment effects on binary outcomes
  5. A 95% confidence interval that excludes 1 indicates statistical significance at 5%
B) A risk ratio below 1 indicates no difference between the groups

Remember. Ratio null = 1. Below 1 = less risk; above 1 = more risk.

Trap. Treating any ratio below 1 as 'no effect'.

Why not the others.
A) The risk ratio is the risk in the treated group divided by the risk in the control group: True: this is the definition.
C) Risk ratios are usually reported with confidence intervals: True: the interval shows precision.

From the figure, what is the median time to conversion for the pooled data?
D) It cannot be determined

Remember. Median time to event = time at which the curve crosses 50%.

Trap. Reading the end of follow-up as the median.

Why not the others.
A) About 12 months: At 12 months about 8% have converted.
B) About 24 months: At 24 months about 16% have converted.

Conversion to bipolar disorder in young people after a first depressive episode: five studies and a pooled curve, with numbers at risk; vertical ticks mark censored participants. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.9.6.4
Which statement is supported by the figure?
  1. At 24 months, cumulative conversion ranges from about 8% to about 30% across studies
  2. About half of young people convert within four years
  3. The spread between studies narrows as follow-up lengthens
  4. No conversions occur in Study 4 after 24 months
  5. Study 3 reports the highest conversion rate
A) At 24 months, cumulative conversion ranges from about 8% to about 30% across studies

Remember. Read values off a curve with a vertical line at the time of interest.

Trap. Reading the pooled curve as if it were every study.

Why not the others.
B) About half of young people convert within four years: The pooled curve reaches only 26% at 48 months.
C) The spread between studies narrows as follow-up lengthens: The spread widens, from 8% to 30% at 24 months to 16% to 42% at 48 months.

13.4 Systematic review and meta-analysis · 13.4.1

A team in Lincoln plans a systematic review of lithium augmentation in treatment-resistant depression.

What is the unit of recruitment in this piece of research?
C) Previously completed studies

Why. Primary research collects new data from participants. Secondary research (systematic review, meta-analysis) takes studies that have already been completed as its raw material, so each included study is the unit that is screened, appraised and, if suitable, pooled.

Remember. Secondary research: the unit of analysis is the study. (Primary recruits people, secondary recruits papers)

Trap. Choosing patients because the review is ultimately about patients.

Why not the others.
A) Individual patients with treatment-resistant depression: Patients are the unit of primary research.
B) Psychiatrists who prescribe lithium: Clinicians might be surveyed in primary research, not here.

✓ Got it↻ Again

13.4 Systematic review and meta-analysis · 13.4.2
Which feature is characteristic of a narrative review rather than a systematic review?
D) Papers are chosen from those the author is familiar with

Why. The defining weakness of a narrative review is that the search is not reproducible. Systematic reviews state the question, search several databases with a documented strategy, apply explicit criteria and report the flow of studies.

Remember. Systematic = explicit, comprehensive, reproducible search. (If you cannot repeat the search, it is not systematic)

Trap. Assuming a well-referenced review must be systematic.

Why not the others.
A) A protocol registered on PROSPERO before searching: Registration is a hallmark of a systematic review.
B) Searches of several databases with a stated strategy: This is what makes a review systematic.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 23
13.4 Systematic review and meta-analysis · 13.4.1
In meta-analyses of treatments in psychiatry, which study design is most often pooled?
E) Randomised controlled trials

Why. Most meta-analyses address treatment questions, and the RCT is the design of choice for these. Observational studies can be pooled, but residual confounding is not removed by pooling, so results need more caution.

Remember. Intervention meta-analysis = pooled RCTs. (Pool the gold standard)

Trap. Thinking meta-analysis can only include RCTs.

Why not the others.
A) Case-control studies: Pooled mainly for aetiology questions.
B) Case series: No comparison group, rarely pooled.

✓ Got it↻ Again

13.4 Systematic review and meta-analysis · 13.4.2

A reviewer searching for trials of digital CBT for insomnia wants to reduce publication bias by including grey literature.

Which source is grey literature?
B) A doctoral thesis held in a university repository

Why. Studies with null results are less likely to reach journals. Searching theses, conference proceedings, trial registries and regulator reports finds some of these and reduces publication bias.

Remember. Grey literature = not commercially published (theses, abstracts, regulatory and trial-registry reports). (Grey = outside the journal shelf)

Trap. Thinking open access or online equals grey.

Why not the others.
A) A trial report in the British Journal of Psychiatry: A peer-reviewed journal article is formal literature.
C) A record found in MEDLINE: MEDLINE indexes published journal literature.

13.4 Systematic review and meta-analysis · 13.4.4

The table summarises a meta-analysis of ten trials of a supplement for ADHD, which reports a significant pooled benefit.

What is the main limitation?
D) Pooling biased studies gives a precise but biased answer

Why. Meta-analysis reduces random error but not systematic error. If every trial overestimates benefit through poor concealment and lack of blinding, the pooled estimate is consistently wrong with a narrow interval.

Remember. Precision is not validity: garbage in, garbage out. (Garbage in, garbage out)

Trap. Mistaking a narrow pooled CI for strong evidence.

Why not the others.
A) The trials should have been weighted equally: Equal weighting would not correct bias and is not standard.
B) Meta-analysis can only include double-blind trials: It can include any design, but quality must be assessed.
